newsitem.title: CHINA: WEEK AHEAD-HK stocks face shakeout amid HK dlr woe.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-HK stocks face shakeout amid HK dlr woe.

text.p: Hong Kong shares could face a major shakeout when the market reopens on Tuesday, with fragile sentiment due to concerns about the Hong Kong dollar likely to be exacerbated by shaky Wall Street stocks, analysts said.
"The Hang Seng Index can fall four to five percent," said Percy Au-Young, director of research at DBS Securities.
"Since the ninth of July, which is when the latest rally started, the market has rallied by about 2,000 points. At this level the market is quite susceptible to profit-taking."

Fears about a speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar, Asia's last major U.S dollar-fixed exchange rate, provoked a slide of 400.83 points, or 2.43 percent, in Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index on Friday to a close of 16,096.88 points.
It was the biggest point decline since June 12, capping a jittery week which saw the blue chip barometer shed 550.66 points, or 3.31 percent, its biggest weekly decline since March.
Hong Kong stocks traded in London later continued the slide, with a drop of 525.39 points, or 3.26 percent, in the Hang Seng London Reference Index to a close of 15,571.49 points.
As the Hong Kong market reopens on Tuesday, following Monday's Sino-Japanese war victory day holiday, it will also have to digest last Friday's slump in U.S. stocks.

The Dow industrials tumbled 247.37 points, or 3.11 percent, on Friday to close at 7,694.66 points, a slide which is likely to rattle nervous investors, particularly ahead of next Tuesday's U.S. Federal Reserve policy-setting meeting.

"If the Dow Jones stabilises on Monday, that could help Hong Kong on Tuesday and minimise the drop, but further weakness could mean a more serious drop for the Hong Kong market," said Kelvin Tang, an analyst at ImPac Asset Management.

With short-term interest rates in Hong Kong jacked higher amid currency concerns, analysts said interest rate sensitive property and banking stocks looked set to take the brunt of any hammering in share prices next week.
"The overnight rate was pushed up to eight percent on Friday, and that is quite high given that it used to be at about five," said Au-Young.

"If short-term rates stay at this high level for a few months, then long-term interest rates will have to go up and that will affect property prices and stock prices too because people would rather put their money in the bank."
But while property and bank stocks might lead the fall, they should be the first to rebound, Au-Young said. He expected the Hang Seng Index to find support at 15,200 to 15,400 points.

Analysts said concerns about the Hong Kong dollar should not last long. "Hong Kong's fundamentals are strong and should not trigger concern over the currency. Hong Kong is different from other Asian countries," said Tang.
Asian currencies have been battered over recent months and the Hong Kong dollar, which has rarely strayed from HK$7.75 to the U.S. dollar, is considered the next obvious choice.
"It's just like a domino effect. But there is nothing bad about Hong Kong's economy or political situation so most people are still very, very confident about the peg," said Au-Young.
"The Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the People's Bank of China have enough power to defend the peg and so long as Hong Kong people remain confident, the peg will be safe," he said.
Analysts said they also expected the U.S. Federal Reserve to leave interest rates unchanged at this coming week's meeting.
"The market should stabilise around 15,200 points and then consolidate between 15,200 and 15,600," said Tang
A drop to 15,200 to 15,400 points would retrace about two thirds of the market's rally since early July, said Au-Young. "After retracing about two-thirds, it will reach good support."
